# LiNGAM regression fixtures

`rcd_baseline.json` holds causal orders and B matrices produced by the **original** FedLiNGAM implementation (github.com/ptorrijos99/FedLiNGAM), the code the PGM 2026 paper links to, on three fixed synthetic problems.

It exists so the port into `fedcausal.lingam` can be shown not to have changed the paper's results. **Do not regenerate it from ported code**: that would make the test compare the port against itself. Regenerate only with `record_baseline.py`, in this directory, pointed at the original repository.

Each case carries eight method records. Four are FedRCD-family solvers: `fedrcd`, `fedrcd_noniterative`, `ishc` (the beta/OLS-deflation ISHC) and `fedrcd_exact`. The other four are comparison baselines: `fedishc` (the published alpha-ratio-deflation ISHC), `fedhc`, `hc_lingam` and `hc`. `fedishc` and `fedhc` are recorded from `src.fedishc.core.ishc` and `src.fedishc.core.hc`, which take aggregated-stats input like the FedRCD family. `hc_lingam` and `hc` are recorded from `src.hclingam.HCLiNGAM(method='hc-lingam' | 'hc').fit(x)` against the **pooled** data matrix directly, since those two are centralised and never see a federated aggregation step. `fedhc`'s original, `hc()` with its default `iterative=False`, returns `None` for B (the no-deflation ablation leaves B estimation to the caller), so that one method's `B` field is recorded as `null` and only its `causal_order` is checked against the port.

Each record also carries `b_sha16`, a 16-hex-char SHA-256 digest of the true coefficient matrix. A consumer that reimplements `make_lingam_data`, such as a test that regenerates these same synthetic problems to check the ported solvers, should hash its own `b_true` the same way and compare against this first. A mismatch means the RNG call sequence desynced (wrong draw order, batched calls) and the data itself differs, so any downstream discrepancy is not a solver bug.

Only `b_true` is safe to hash. It comes from `random`, `uniform` and `choice`, which scale raw bits, so its bytes are the same everywhere. Two other arrays are not, for the same underlying reason in different libraries:

- `x` is built by `x @ b_true[j]`, and BLAS takes its summation order and FMA use from whichever kernel the host CPU dispatches to.
- `noise` comes from `laplace`, an inverse-CDF transform through `log`, and libm's `log` differs by an ulp between platforms. `noise_sha16` is still recorded, as a record of what the recording machine saw, but nothing asserts it: the digest agrees on Windows and disagrees on Linux while the values themselves match to ~1e-16.

Both are pinned portably, to 1e-12, by the `cumulants` field below. That is the check that would actually catch a desync, since a wrong draw order moves the cumulants by far more than an ulp.

Each record also carries `cumulants`, the aggregated statistics (`cov`, `c3`, `c12`, `c21`, `c4`, `c13`, `c31`, `c22`, each as nested lists) that `aggregate_and_compute_cumulants` produced from the original implementation for that problem. This field is per-*case*, not per-method: all four method records sharing a `name` carry an identical `cumulants` block, the same way they share the draw digests. It exists because once a causal order is fixed, every solver re-estimates `B` from `cov` alone and never reads the higher-order cumulants again, so a small bias-correction error in `cumulants.py` (a slightly wrong constant, a dropped term that mostly cancels) would only surface in the causal-order/`B` comparison if it happened to be large enough to flip the tau ranking. Pinning the eight arrays directly closes that gap: it catches a cumulant regression even when it is too small to change any solver's output.
